The story behind an idea

The self-fulfilling prophecy

If everyone believes a bank will fail, it ends up failing. An idea from the sociologist Robert Merton.

In 1948, the sociologist Robert K. Merton coined the phrase self-fulfilling prophecy. His example was a sound bank during the Great Depression: if a rumour spreads that it is about to fail, customers withdraw their money en masse and the bank really fails. The false belief brings about its own fulfilment.

From economics to daily life

Merton drew on the "Thomas theorem": if people define situations as real, they are real in their consequences. The idea was later applied to school (the Pygmalion effect), relationships and stereotypes.

For example, if someone expects another person to be unfriendly, they may treat them coldly, and that coldness draws out the distant response that confirms the expectation. Not everything we expect comes true, but our expectations do change the way we act.

References

  1. Merton, R. K. (1948). The self-fulfilling prophecy. The Antioch Review, 8(2), 193–210.
